questions.q: Before flagging a missing row in a price series as a data gap, what should you check first?
options: Whether the price on that date would have been round-numbered
Whether the date was actually a trading day on the relevant exchange's calendar, not a weekend or holiday
Whether the ticker symbol has exactly 4 characters
Whether the previous day's volume was above average
questions.explain: Not every calendar day is a trading day. Comparing missing dates against the actual exchange trading calendar (e.g., via pandas_market_calendars) distinguishes real data gaps from expected non-trading days.

questions.q: Why is a rolling median and median absolute deviation (MAD) generally preferred over a rolling mean and standard deviation for detecting bad ticks?
options: MAD is faster to compute in all cases
Mean and standard deviation are themselves heavily distorted by the very outliers being searched for, while median/MAD are more robust to them
Standard deviation cannot be computed on return data
MAD only works on prices, never on returns
questions.explain: A single large outlier can substantially distort a rolling mean and standard deviation, making threshold-based detection less reliable. Median and MAD are far less sensitive to the extreme values being flagged.

questions.q: A return series shows a single day with an extremely large move. Should it automatically be treated as a bad tick and removed?
options: Yes, any return beyond 3 standard deviations should always be removed
No — Lesson 3 established that real financial returns have fat tails, so large moves do occur; flagged points should be manually reviewed, not automatically dropped
Yes, because real markets never move more than 2% in a day
It depends only on the day of the week
questions.explain: Fat tails are a genuine stylized fact of financial returns. A flagged outlier might be a real event (earnings surprise, M&A news) rather than bad data, so manual review before removal is essential.

questions.q: Why is setting a `limit` on `ffill()` (forward-fill) important when reindexing prices to a trading calendar?
options: It makes the computation run faster with no effect on correctness
Without a limit, a long real data outage could be silently papered over with a long run of fabricated 'flat' days
It is required by pandas and the function will error without it
It converts simple returns into log returns automatically
questions.explain: An unlimited forward-fill will happily fill an arbitrarily long gap with a repeated stale value, disguising a real, extended outage as legitimate flat pricing. Limiting the fill forces genuine large gaps to remain visible.

questions.q: What does a long run of identical consecutive prices most likely indicate about an instrument?
options: The instrument is extremely high-volume and liquid
The price feed vendor made a currency conversion error
The instrument may be illiquid or not actually trading, rather than genuinely flat in value
The instrument has just undergone a stock split
questions.explain: A stale price run (the same price repeated for many consecutive observations) more often reflects an illiquid instrument that simply isn't trading, rather than a value that is genuinely unchanged day after day.
